caption:
My face was on the homepage of THE NEW YORK TIMES!!! 🎉

I’m so excited that I’ve been featured in an article in the New York Times that talks about a topic near and dear to my heart: the impact of ADHD on money management 🔥

I ended up in $15K worth of debt because I couldn’t stop impulse spending, and couldn’t get my finances under control. 

I felt guilty and shameful. I felt like something was wrong with me.

I spent so many years trying to shame myself into spending less and being better with my money, but I’ve realized that I just need a different approach. 

Nothing was wrong with me, I just had ADHD.

Being “good with money” when you have ADHD is not about having more willpower, or being more disciplined. 

It’s about accepting and unlearning the expectations of how you you “should” be managing your money, because the majority of traditional finance education written for and by neurotypical folks.

It’s not your fault, you were just never given the tools to succeed 💚

Thank you @paulettejperhach for writing this article. It was so needed.

This is such important representation for everyone with ADHD who feel like something is wrong with them and I am so honoured to be a part of that.

PS. There’s an entire chapter of my book dedicated to talking about ADHD and money. I share more of my story, help you work through the shame, and provide tips for moving forward. Preorder is now available 👀💸

How has your ADHD impacted your money? Let me know in the comments!! ⬇️

If our goal was having the highest net worth possible then it made more sense to keep renting. But the reasons why we wanted a home had nothing to do with the money. 

We didn’t buy because “renting is throwing money away” (it’s not).
We didn’t buy to build equity.
We didn’t buy as a financial “investment.”

We bought for emotional reasons 💕

We wanted stability. A community where we knew our neighbours, a yard for our future dog to run, and no fear of being forced to move.

We wanted a space that was ours. Where we could paint the walls whatever color we wanted, make major changes without asking permission, and adapt the home to meet our needs.

The math doesn’t lie—a house is typically not a great financial investment. But that doesn’t mean buying a home is a bad decision 🫶🏻

caption:
I reduced my impulsive spending and now I have savings, investments for retirement, and a house 😳

Okay but seriously, it did take me a long time to break this “habit” and I want to share some of the tips that worked for me because “just stop buying things” is not helpful lol.

The key is adding friction to make it harder to spend, while simultaneously rewiring your brain to crave a different source of dopamine. 

Ways to add friction ⬇️

🚧 unsubscribe from promotional emails 
🚧 remove Apple Pay and auto saved credit card #’s from phone/ computer 
🚧 give yourself a monthly spending allowance 
🚧 delete apps you tend to spend on like DoorDash 
🚧 give yourself “rules” like waiting 24h before purchasing 

Ways to get dopamine for FREE ⬇️

✨ add items to a wishlist
✨ get free media from your local library
✨ learn something new
✨ brainstorm on Pinterest
✨ join a local buy nothing FB group
✨ create something 
✨ move your body 

If you want more ideas—my previous post is all about how to create a dopamine menu for yourself 👀

caption:
3 ways to make saving money more fun 🤑🎲

1️⃣ Sticker charts 

I’m such a huge fan of sticker charts, and so are all of my clients! It might seem “childish” to some of you, but that’s honestly what makes it so fun 💃🏻

You can them set guidelines for yourself- like for every $50 saved, a sticker goes up. If you’re saving a large sum of money, break it down into smaller chunks. 

Reward yourself for reaching milestones ⭐️ This does not have to be a monetary reward, and could be as simple as cooking your favourite meal, or giving yourself a Saturday of self care. 

2️⃣ Visual progress trackers 

Being able to visually see your saving progress is a great motivator to keep saving!! We can turn this into more of a game by using trackers that you have to colour in. Kind of like an adult colouring sheet, but for your money! Use some fun pens or markers and watch your savings tracker come to life. 

3️⃣ Saving challenges

Grab your bestie or significant other and start a savings challenge with them! This can look like seeing how much you can each save in x amount of time, or seeing who can save x amount the quickest. Set up weekly or monthly accountability check-ins with each other and of course, make sure to come up with a reward at the end! Maybe you can go out for a nice dinner together after the challenge. 

Let me know in the comments which one you’re going to try out!! ⬇️

Here’s exactly how to make your own Dopamine Menu ✨

A Dopamine Menu is a list of feel-good activities that you can reach for the next time you’re feeling like you need that hit of dopamine. If you struggle with impulsive spending—this is a great tool you can use to get dopamine without hurting your wallet 🤑

The goal is to replace the habit of shopping with a different habit that doesn’t cost you anything.

We’re harnessing habit formation theory here, so we want to reduce as much friction as possible!! A great way to achieve this is by making the cue (the dopamine menu) as visible as possible. AKA post it on your fridge, or make your phone background so that you are constantly seeing it 👀

An easy, low effort way to get started is by making your Dopamine Menu in your notes app or jotting it down on paper. It doesn’t have to be aesthetic to be effective 🫶🏻

caption:
As someone who is burnt out & neurodivergent—I severely underestimated how much my open loops affect me 🔁😅

Open loops are incomplete tasks or unresolved problems. They are things that you need to complete and therefore need to remember to do.

Our brains become overloaded—which makes it hard to focus & drains our energy. We are experiencing too much stimuli, too many options, too much input. It’s like running your computer with 100+ tabs open all the time. And they will continue to occupy mental space until the loop is closed.

I realized how much this impacting my ability to work & I decided to intentionally dedicate time to tackle these tasks every day. I’m not being dramatic when I say this practice has already changed my life 🥹

Since I’ve started implementing ✨close the loop time✨ I’ve noticed that I have an easier time focusing the rest of the day & have more energy overall. My morning starts with a win and a dopamine hit that I can ride into my work tasks 🏄‍♀️

I’d love to know if you try this strategy out & how it goes for you 🫶🏻

If you’re also feeling anxious about setting 2026 goals, you’re not alone 💚

When I first started my business, everything felt exciting–I was posting multiple times a day with ease, and I felt really connected to my community. I had a clear vision of what I was creating and what my goals were.

But somewhere along the line I lost sight of who I was and what I wanted. The goals I had set when I started my business no longer felt aligned. Posting content online for years and opening myself up to being perceived, judged, and misunderstood slowly eroded my mental health. 

Now, I’m burnt out and exhausted. I feel disconnected from this community, from YOU—the reason I started creating content in the first place. And while I don’t necessarily have any solutions, I wanted to be honest about how I’m feeling. 

It’s hard feeling so lost at a time where it appears like everyone else is sure of where they are going. But I promise that you’re not the only one feeling this way. 

What if we reframed “being lost”? Instead of viewing it as a bad thing—think of it as an opportunity to evolve and change. Maybe it’s a sign to step into a different version of yourself 🫶🏻

I don’t need to set specific goals right now because I’m still figuring things out, and that’s okay. Instead, I’m going to focus on reconnecting with myself, my business, and with this community. I hope you’ll stick around in the meantime 💕

Want more details on how investing works? Keep reading ⬇️

Investing is one of the most powerful tools for building wealth because you don’t need to make a lot of money to reap the benefits. This is because compound interest will grow the money you invest into even more money. 

Here’s how compound interest works 👉🏻let’s say you have $500 invested and you’re earning 7% interest on it per year. In year 1, you’ll have earned $35 of interest so your new balance is $535. But then the next year, you’re earning 7% interest on $535 instead of $500. So in year 2 you’ll earn $38 of interest so your new total is $573. Essentially, your money keeps growing, and as a result you continue earning interest on a bigger and bigger amount. 

Now that you understand compound interest a bit better, let’s get into the 3 investing steps 🤑

Step 1️⃣: open an investment account like a TFSA or RRSP. 

Step 2️⃣: fund your investment account. I recommend automating this step so that you’re consistently contributing each month. 

Step 3️⃣: purchase your investments. Choose from assets such as stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, and more.

Do you really need it? Or is it just consumerism? 🛍

The basis of consumer culture is the assumption that we can find fulfilment and sense of self through the products we buy.

Brands know this, and they specifically market to your insecurities while handing you the remedy on a silver platter. Purchase this product and you’ll be one step closer to who you want to be.

Or maybe you’re swiping your card as a coping mechanism. Turning to retail therapy in an attempt to mask feelings of sadness, jealously, anxiety, stress, or loneliness. Or you’re neurodivergent like me and you really just need some dopamine 🧠

Next time you feel like you need to buy something—ask yourself why you’re feeling tempted 💸 Understanding why we do certain things with our money is the key the changing them 👀

And maybe you’ll realize that you didn’t need that new thing, you really just needed to feel something 💚

caption:
Confused on what your financial priorities should be? READ THIS ⬇️

I created this flow chart as an easy way to break down and simplify the order of your financial priorities!!

1️⃣ Are your monthly bills covered?

The first place your money should be going each month is to your living expenses which include all of your bills, fixed expenses, necessary living expenses and minimum debt payments. 

If your bills currently aren’t being covered (or are being put on your credit card) then THIS is your financial priority. 💸

Focus on lowering your expenses and increasing your income if possible.

2️⃣ Do you have a 3-6 month safety fund?

After you make sure all your monthly essentials are covered, your next priority should be saving up a safety fund aka an emergency fund.

Yes, even before tackling your debt.

If you don’t currently have a full safety fund- THIS is your financial priority. 💸

3️⃣ Do you have any high interest (≥8%) debt?

Now that you have a safety fund built up, you can focus on aggressively paying down your high-interest debt.

If you have high interest debt, and you’ve got #1 and #2 covered, then THIS is your financial priority. 💸

4️⃣ Do you have any low interest (≤7%) debt?

If you have low interest debt, you can actually balance paying this off while also saving and investing your money! 💸

You don’t need to wait until you’re low interest debt free to start investing 🔥

5️⃣ Is there anything you’re saving for in the next 5-7 years?

This would include saving for sinking funds and upcoming financial goals like a down payment on a home.

If yes, then you can focus on saving AND investing.
If no, then your main priority can be investing.

Ultimately this flowchart is just a starting point, and everyone’s situation will be different because finance is personal 👀

Which financial priority are you focusing on right now?
